newsitem.title: USA: CIA warned of possible chemical exposure - Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: CIA warned of possible chemical exposure - Pentagon.

text.p: Despite a CIA warning in 1991 about the possible exposure of U.S. troops to Iraqi nerve gas, mistakes by the Army and intelligence officials caused a long delay in investigating the incident, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.

"Clearly there were missed opportunities," a senior defence official told reporters in releasing a detailed report on the destruction by 82nd Airborne Division engineers of an Iraqi ammunition dump at Kamisiyah in March 1991.
Bernard Rostker told reporters the CIA informed the Army in November 1991 that U.S. troops had apparently been involved in the destruction and that the Iraqis said chemical arms were there.

But the Army subsequently misidentified U.S. troops in southern Iraq when the thousands of chemical rockets were destroyed, and U.S. intelligence officials did not believe Iraqi statements about the arms. The investigation was dropped until 1994, the report said.

Rostker stressed that there was still no proof that any U.S. troops were exposed to nerve agents from the destruction and that, at any rate, the controversial event did not provide an answer to the mystery of Gulf War illness.
"I don't know whether it (the report) gets us that much closer ... it isn't the magic answer to Gulf War illness," he told reporters at a news conference.

Gulf War troops have complained of symptoms ranging from memory loss to muscle aches, and the Pentagon last year notified 20,000 veterans that they may have suffered low-level exposure from blast clouds drifting away from Kamisiyah.

Under orders from President Bill Clinton, the Defence Department is conducting an intense investigation of Gulf War illness, although experts have concluded that no common cause of Gulf medical complaints exists.

Rostker said the CIA had informed the Army in late 1991 that U.N. inspectors found U.S. military equipment at Kamisiyah and that Iraqi officials had told the United Nations that chemical arms were there.
But he said the U.S. intelligence community did not believe the Iraqis, another major reason why the information on U.S. troop presence was not quickly and thoroughly investigated.
"We (now) accept the conclusion that there were American units that blew up Kamisiyah ... that our troops, in fact, blew up those chemicals," Rostker told reporters.

The new report also revealed that U.S. intelligence had reason to believe earlier in 1991 that chemical arms were present at Kamisiyah. But Rostker would not discuss that issue, saying the CIA had refused to declassify the source of such information.
"We cannot publish when we get against the firewall" of secrecy, he said, adding that he had pressed the spy agency to release the information, to no avail.

The interim report appeared to conflict with earlier Pentagon statements that the military had little indication that U.S. troops might have been exposed to nerve agents in blasts set off by the engineers at Kamisiyah on March 4 and 10, 1991.

The U.S. Army's Central Command in 1991 incorrectly identified U.S. troops in the area as members of the 24th Mechanized Infantry Division, the report said, and when that was not confirmed the matter was dropped until more recently.
